section_summary: This section combines policy memoranda, corporate correspondence, consular reporting, and public appeals concerning American exports of scrap iron, petroleum, gasoline components, refinery equipment, and technical information to Japan and the Soviet Union. Much of the January 1940 correspondence documents the State Department’s informal “moral embargo” on technology for producing high-quality aviation gasoline and its effort to collect company-by-company export data. Other major items include a 1939 report on how the Dutch East Indies might respond to an American oil embargo, observations of a Japanese freighter loading Mexican lead at Brownsville, and congressional correspondence urging restrictions on war-material exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: White House memorandum requesting a reply on scrap-iron exports
subfiles.to: Under Secretary of State Sumner Welles
subfiles.about: Requests preparation of a memorandum replying to an inquiry about scrap-iron exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: President Roosevelt forwards the matter to the Under Secretary of State for preparation of a reply. The brief White House memorandum initiates the ensuing exchange concerning figures on scrap-iron exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Hornbeck to prepare the President’s memorandum
subfiles.about: Directs Hornbeck to prepare the memorandum requested by the President.
subfiles.summary: The Under Secretary asks Dr. Hornbeck to draft the desired memorandum. The instruction directly follows Roosevelt’s request of October 22.

subfiles.title: Hiss memorandum transmitting material on scrap-iron exports
subfiles.about: Transmits a factual memorandum and draft presidential reply concerning scrap-iron exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hiss explains that Hornbeck has supplied a one-page memorandum entitled “Exports of Scrap Iron to Japan” and a draft transmittal to the President. Because the Roosevelt-Steiger correspondence refers to official figures only for scrap iron, he considers this sufficient to answer Mrs. Roosevelt’s request for facts.

subfiles.title: Draft reply from Welles to the President
subfiles.about: Drafts a transmittal of facts on scrap-iron exports for Eleanor Roosevelt.
subfiles.summary: The draft encloses a brief memorandum containing the essential facts about scrap-iron exports to Japan. It also refers to Welles’s September 30 memorandum to Mrs. Roosevelt on United States-Japanese trade since the outbreak of Sino-Japanese hostilities.

subfiles.title: Welles letter to President Roosevelt on scrap-iron exports
subfiles.about: Sends the President a brief factual memorandum for Mrs. Roosevelt on scrap-iron exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Welles provides the requested brief account of scrap-iron exports to Japan. He notes that his more extensive September 30 memorandum on United States-Japanese trade may also assist Mrs. Roosevelt in answering Mrs. Steiger.

subfiles.title: Reply to Mrs. Cleary on export controls
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the licensing controls applicable to scrap iron and other strategic exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that the Export Control Act of July 2, 1940 authorized restrictions on iron and steel scrap, metals, aviation gasoline, lubricating oil, and other materials. He assures Cleary that licenses are denied when exports would harm national defense and that controls are continually adjusted as conditions change.

subfiles.title: Routing notation marked Greene
subfiles.about: Records a brief routing or filing notation associated with the surrounding correspondence.
subfiles.summary: The page contains only the name Greene and the notation SA/GRN. No substantive message or date survives in the OCR.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs summary of Batavia despatch 312
subfiles.about: Summarizes Dutch East Indies officials’ expected response to a possible American embargo on strategic materials for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Officials in the Dutch East Indies reportedly believed they would have to continue selling petroleum, tin, and nickel to Japan to avoid attack and occupation of the Borneo and Sumatra oil fields. The memorandum notes the anomaly that an American-owned Socony-Vacuum subsidiary might supply Japan with oil denied by the United States, while recording Dickover’s support for an embargo.

subfiles.title: Despatch 312 on Dutch East Indies opinion regarding an embargo on Japan
subfiles.from: Erle R. Dickover, American Consul General at Batavia
subfiles.about: Reports official Dutch East Indies views on the consequences of a United States embargo on war materials for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Dickover reports that senior military and economic officials feared an American petroleum embargo could prompt Japan to seize oil fields at Tarakan, Balikpapan, and elsewhere in Borneo and Sumatra. They therefore expected the Dutch East Indies to sell Japan the needed oil, even at the cost of refining profits, to preserve neutrality and reduce the risk of attack. The despatch evaluates regional oil production, Japan’s requirements, refinery compatibility, and the position of Royal Dutch-Shell and Socony-Vacuum interests. Dickover nevertheless concludes that the United States should impose an embargo and prepare for the resulting complications.

subfiles.title: Letter to Gregory enclosing the aviation-gasoline policy statement
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Encloses the State Department’s December 20, 1939 statement on withholding aviation-gasoline technology from certain countries.
subfiles.summary: Green sends Gregory a copy of the Department’s public statement on further delivery of plans, plants, manufacturing rights, and technical information for producing high-quality aviation gasoline. The letter presents the statement for Gregory’s information without additional interpretation.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for moral-embargo material
subfiles.about: Records the transfer of document 894.24/776B to the moral-embargo file.
subfiles.summary: The sheet states that the item was transferred to decimal file 700.00116 Moral Embargo/60A. It contains no substantive correspondence beyond that filing instruction.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Hargrove telephone call on lubricating-oil equipment
subfiles.about: Records an inquiry on whether exporting lubricating-oil rerunning equipment to Japan conflicted with aviation-gasoline policy.
subfiles.summary: George Hargrove reported that E. B. Badger and Company had Japanese orders for equipment used to rerun lubricating oils and sought confirmation that filling them would not violate government policy. Green reiterated the December 14 explanation and December 20 statement, leaving each company to judge whether a transaction fell within the policy. Hargrove said the equipment was unrelated to aviation gasoline and that the company would probably fill its orders.

subfiles.title: Charge slip for file 894.24
subfiles.about: Records the later administrative charging of an enclosure from file 894.24.
subfiles.summary: The slip charges an enclosure, identified with the notation 7781, to PED-Breakey. It is a postwar file-control record rather than substantive policy correspondence.

subfiles.title: Foster Wheeler letter on oil-refinery equipment for Japan and Russia
subfiles.from: Harry S. Brown, Foster Wheeler Corporation
subfiles.about: States Foster Wheeler’s understanding that it should not quote refinery equipment to Japan or Russia without permission.
subfiles.summary: Brown says H. J. Halle informed Foster Wheeler of his State Department conversations. The company reports that it has no outstanding quotations to Japan or Russia and will issue none without express permission.

subfiles.title: Green reply clarifying policy for Foster Wheeler
subfiles.about: Clarifies that the government policy concerns only technology required for high-quality aviation gasoline.
subfiles.summary: Green acknowledges Brown’s letter and encloses the December 20, 1939 press release. He emphasizes that the policy applies only to plans, plants, rights, and technical information needed to produce high-quality aviation gasoline.

subfiles.title: Sun Oil letter referring the Department to E. B. Badger
subfiles.from: J. Howard Pew, Sun Oil Company
subfiles.about: Explains that Sun Oil is not directly engaged in the specified technical activities and refers the inquiry to E. B. Badger and Sons.
subfiles.summary: Pew states that Sun Oil itself does not conduct the activities described in Green’s memorandum. Because Sun holds a minority interest in Houdry Process Corporation, it forwarded the Department’s letter to E. B. Badger and Sons, Houdry’s exclusive licensing agent.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Sun Oil Company
subfiles.from: Department of State, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: J. Howard Pew, Sun Oil Company
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Sun Oil’s referral of the technical-policy inquiry to E. B. Badger and Sons.
subfiles.summary: The Department notes Sun Oil’s statement that it is not engaged in the activities covered by the December 19 memorandum. It also records that the company forwarded the matter to E. B. Badger and Sons for consideration.

subfiles.title: Tuttle report on hydro-polymer gasoline exports
subfiles.about: Reports 1939 exports and 1940 commitments for hydro-polymer gasoline and blended crude oil sold to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Tuttle reports no blending-agent sales to the Soviet Union but states that 50,414 barrels of hydro-polymer gasoline were sold to Asano Bussan Company for Japan in 1939, with approximately 4,500 barrels committed for 1940. He also describes small quantities used in large blended-crude shipments and stresses that those transactions did not constitute separate sales of hydro-polymer gasoline.

subfiles.title: Green request for continuing reports from Tuttle’s company
subfiles.about: Requests monthly or shipment-by-shipment reports of blending-agent exports to Japan and the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Green acknowledges Tuttle’s information on 1939 blending-agent exports. He asks the company to continue reporting such exports monthly or whenever shipments occur.

subfiles.title: Charge slip referencing documents 780 and 781
subfiles.about: Records the later charging of enclosures associated with documents 780 and 781.
subfiles.summary: The slip lists file references 780, 781A, and 781B and charges the enclosure to PED-Breakey. It is an administrative record created after the substantive correspondence.

subfiles.title: Representative O’Neal letter requesting an export-policy statement
subfiles.about: Forwards a church protest and asks whether legislation is needed to stop war-material exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: O’Neal sends Hull a letter from the pastor of the Eighteenth Street Baptist Church, describing it as one of many similar communications. He requests a statement on relations with Japan and on whether new legislation is required to halt war-material exports.

subfiles.title: Eighteenth Street Baptist Church appeal for action against Japan
subfiles.from: M. P. Hunt and W. A. Colvin, Eighteenth Street Baptist Church
subfiles.about: Calls for an end to American munitions exports and a consumer boycott of Japanese goods.
subfiles.summary: The church condemns Japan’s war in China as a violation of international agreements and protests American provision of war supplies. It asks the President, Secretary Hull, and Congress to stop the trade and urges a boycott of Japanese imports, especially silk and silk stockings. The resolution had been adopted unanimously on December 24.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Representative O’Neal
subfiles.about: Explains the limited statutory authority for prohibiting exports to Japan and returns the church letter.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that the Neutrality Act did not authorize a ban on arms exports to belligerents and that existing law covered only limited commodities such as tin-plate scrap and helium. It advises that new legislation would be needed to prohibit exports of other manufactured goods or raw materials such as scrap iron. Hunt’s letter is returned as requested.

subfiles.title: Standard Oil of Indiana report of no blending-agent exports
subfiles.from: C. T. Bergeson, Standard Oil Company of Indiana
subfiles.to: Department of State, attention Joseph C. Green
subfiles.about: Reports no 1939 sales of blending agents to Japan or the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Standard Oil of Indiana states that its records show no blending-agent sales to either destination during 1939. The company offers to cooperate with future information requests.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Standard Oil of Indiana
subfiles.from: Department of State, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: C. T. Bergeson, Standard Oil Company of Indiana
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the company’s report of no blending-agent exports to Japan or the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: The Department records Standard Oil’s statement that it made no relevant sales during 1939. The letter is a brief formal acknowledgment of the company’s cooperation.

subfiles.title: Cities Service report of no blending-agent exports
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, attention Joseph C. Green
subfiles.about: Reports that Cities Service made no sales of specified gasoline blending agents to Japan or the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Cities Service explains the corporate succession from Cities Service Export Oil Company to its own export department. It states that it sold no tetraethyl lead, iso-octane, neo-hexane, or alkylates to Japan or the Soviet Union during 1939.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Cities Service Oil Company
subfiles.from: Department of State, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Cities Service’s report of no relevant exports during 1939.
subfiles.summary: The Department notes that Cities Service exported none of the listed blending agents to Japan or the Soviet Union. The acknowledgment summarizes the products as tetraethyl lead, iso-octane, neo-hexane, and alkylates.

subfiles.title: Sinclair Refining report of no specified exports
subfiles.from: L. V. Stanford, Sinclair Refining Company
subfiles.about: Reports no sales to Japan or the Soviet Union of the products listed in Green’s December 19 inquiry.
subfiles.summary: Sinclair states that it made no sales of the specified products to either Japan or the Soviet Union. The letter is a concise response to the Department’s company survey.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Sinclair Refining Company
subfiles.from: Department of State, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: L. V. Stanford, Sinclair Refining Company
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Sinclair’s report that it made no specified sales to Japan or the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: The Department records Sinclair’s negative response to the December 19 inquiry. The letter contains no additional policy guidance.

subfiles.title: Proctor request for confidential handling
subfiles.about: Requests confidential treatment of Gulf Oil’s blending-agent export information.
subfiles.summary: Although most of the text is lost in the OCR, the surviving letterhead, signature, and subsequent reply identify this as Proctor’s January 5 follow-up. It asks that Gulf Oil’s previously supplied export information be kept confidential.

subfiles.title: Green reply to Proctor on Gulf Oil exports
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Gulf Oil’s export data, promises confidentiality, and requests continuing reports.
subfiles.summary: Green notes Gulf Oil’s past exports and its imminent shipment of one million gallons of iso-octane 95 to Japan. He asks for monthly or shipment-by-shipment reports of blending-agent exports to Japan and the Soviet Union and assures Proctor that the information will remain confidential.

subfiles.title: Gulf Oil report on iso-octane exports to Japan
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, attention Joseph C. Green
subfiles.about: Reports Gulf Oil’s 1939 iso-octane exports and an imminent additional shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Proctor reports no relevant exports to the Soviet Union and no Japanese exports of tetraethyl lead, neo-hexane, or alkylates during 1939. Gulf Oil did export one million gallons of iso-octane 95 to Japan in 1939 and expected to ship another million gallons shortly, with no further commitments then outstanding.

subfiles.title: Leas & McVitty request for petroleum-export information
subfiles.about: Requests figures and company names for exports of aviation gasoline and special lubricating oils to Japan or Russia.
subfiles.summary: Whitmore thanks Yost for an earlier response and asks for additional petroleum-export information. The company seeks both quantities and the identities of American exporters serving Japan or the Soviet Union.

subfiles.title: Yost reply directing Leas & McVitty to the Commerce Department
subfiles.about: States that the State Department lacks the requested export information and identifies another government source.
subfiles.summary: Yost says the State Department does not possess the requested data on aviation gasoline and special lubricating-oil exports. He recommends contacting the Fuel Section of the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce in the Department of Commerce.

subfiles.title: Matamoros despatch on the Akagi Maru loading lead
subfiles.from: Herndon W. Goforth, American Consul at Matamoros
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese ship loading about 2,000 tons of Mexican lead at Brownsville and notes nearby scrap metal.
subfiles.summary: Goforth reports observing the Japanese motor ship Akagi Maru loading approximately 2,000 tons of ASARCO-marked lead bars at Port Brownsville. He also saw a large pile of scrap iron and steel, although local information suggested that New York dealers owned it and that it might not be destined for Japan. The ship was expected to sail through Port Arthur and the Panama Canal to Yokohama, Osaka, and Kobe.

subfiles.title: Brownsville Herald clipping on the Akagi Maru
subfiles.about: Describes the Akagi Maru’s Brownsville visit, cargo operations, officers, and projected voyage to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The clipping profiles Captain H. Tanaka’s drawings and identifies officers N. Takahashi and M. Kurimoto with shipping agent Gilbert Philen. It reports that the Akagi Maru was loading at Brownsville for Yokohama, Osaka, and Kobe and would sail by way of Port Arthur and Cristóbal. Additional columns describe other port traffic, the NYK Line’s worldwide service, and the ship’s significance as an early Japanese vessel to visit a Lower Rio Grande Valley port.

subfiles.title: Moseley memorandum on conversations with Universal Oil Products
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Green and Department of State files
subfiles.about: Records discussions of refinery projects in Japan, contacts with Soviet engineers, and suspended aviation-gasoline technology transfers.
subfiles.summary: Moseley first reassured H. J. Halle that three Universal Oil Products employees and their families were safe in Moscow. Halle withdrew an erroneous claim that Mitsui had received United States permission for a motor-gasoline refinery project, but said his company would probably proceed because the processes did not concern aviation gasoline. Moseley reiterated that companies must judge proposed transactions under the December 20 policy, including preliminary talks with Soviet engineers. Halle also described a nearly completed aviation-gasoline contract with Japan Gasoline Company that Universal had suspended and cited earlier government letters permitting foreign commercial exploitation of its processes.

subfiles.title: Universal Oil Products inquiry about a Mitsui refinery project
subfiles.from: H. J. Halle, Universal Oil Products Company
subfiles.about: Seeks clarification on whether Universal may submit plans for a Mitsui motor-gasoline refinery installation.
subfiles.summary: Halle reports Saneyoshi’s claim that Mitsui had government permission to install equipment for cracking, hot-clay treatment, and nonselective polymerization producing motor rather than aviation gasoline. He asks the Department to verify the claim and advise whether detailed drawings and plans may be submitted.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Halle on Japanese and Soviet negotiations
subfiles.from: Division of Controls, Department of State
subfiles.about: Clarifies the absence of government approval for Mitsui and restates policy for Japanese and Soviet technical negotiations.
subfiles.summary: The Department confirms that neither it, the Army and Navy Munitions Board, nor the War Department had authorized Mitsui’s proposed refinery installation. It again leaves Universal to decide whether motor-gasoline plans would violate the December 20 policy against supplying high-quality aviation-gasoline technology. The reply notes that George E. Shelton had already left Japan and advises that discussions with Soviet engineers should also be governed by the published policy.

subfiles.title: Tide Water report on blending agents and Mitsubishi Oil
subfiles.from: George J. Murray Jr., Tide Water Associated Oil Company
subfiles.about: Reports no current blending-agent exports while describing the company’s Japanese refinery interest and crude-oil sales.
subfiles.summary: Murray states that Tide Water neither manufactured nor exported tetraethyl lead, iso-octane, neo-hexane, or alkylates, though it was considering construction of an alkylate plant. He describes Tide Water’s half ownership of Mitsubishi Oil Company’s Kawasaki refinery and its sales of specially blended crude oil through Mitsubishi interests. He adds that future blends might incorporate alkylates if the proposed plant were built.

subfiles.title: Yost request for future Tide Water alkylate reports
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Tide Water’s negative report and requests notice of future alkylate exports.
subfiles.summary: Yost records Tide Water’s statement that it had made no exports of the specified blending agents to Japan or the Soviet Union. Because the company was considering an alkylate plant, he asks it to report any future exports to those countries.

subfiles.title: Green acknowledgment of E. B. Badger’s suspended negotiations
subfiles.to: E. B. Badger and Sons Company
subfiles.about: Thanks the company for suspending negotiations involving aviation-gasoline plans and technology.
subfiles.summary: Green acknowledges Badger’s statement that it had halted negotiations with interests in certain countries. He expresses appreciation for the company’s cooperation with the government policy on high-quality aviation-gasoline technology.

subfiles.title: Universal Oil Products letter transmitting earlier government approvals
subfiles.from: H. J. Halle, Universal Oil Products Company
subfiles.to: Division of Controls, attention Harold W. Moseley
subfiles.about: Encloses 1937 and 1938 government letters concerning foreign installation of Universal’s iso-octane process.
subfiles.summary: Universal supplies copies of a September 1938 State Department letter and a June 1937 War Department letter. Both enclosures concern licensing and installing the company’s iso-octane process in foreign countries.

subfiles.title: Copy of State Department letter on foreign iso-octane installations
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Controls
subfiles.about: States that the War and Navy Departments had no military-secrecy objection to foreign installation of Universal’s iso-octane process.
subfiles.summary: Yost reports the Acting Secretary of War’s conclusion that military secrecy and national-defense concerns did not preclude installation of the process in any foreign country. The letter also conveys the War and Navy Departments’ appreciation of Universal’s decision to seek government review.

subfiles.title: Copy of War Department letter on toluene and iso-octane processes
subfiles.from: Harry H. Woodring, Secretary of War
subfiles.about: Declines government acquisition of process patents and permits their commercial exploitation at home or abroad.
subfiles.summary: Woodring thanks Universal for offering to assign patents for new toluene and iso-octane processes to prevent foreign dissemination. He explains that industry is better equipped to finance and develop the processes and that broad domestic industrial knowledge is important for wartime production. The War Department therefore raises no objection to commercial exploitation in the United States or abroad.

subfiles.title: Yost acknowledgment of Universal’s historical letters
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the enclosed 1937 and 1938 government letters.
subfiles.summary: Yost confirms receipt of the State Department and War Department letters supplied by Universal Oil Products. The acknowledgment offers no new ruling on their relationship to the 1939 policy.

subfiles.title: Ethyl Gasoline Corporation letter on export reporting
subfiles.from: Ralph C. Champlin, Ethyl Gasoline Corporation
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, attention Joseph C. Green
subfiles.about: Explains that the company will report concentrated Ethyl Fluid shipments but not incomplete aviation-gasoline figures.
subfiles.summary: Champlin says Ethyl Gasoline Corporation’s information on aviation-gasoline shipments to Japan is incomplete and would duplicate more comprehensive reports from exporters. The company will instead provide its records of concentrated Ethyl Fluid shipments from the United States to Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply to Ethyl Gasoline Corporation
subfiles.about: Accepts the proposed reporting arrangement and requests Ethyl Fluid reports for Japan and the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: The Department agrees that Ethyl need not supply its incomplete aviation-gasoline data. It requests continuing reports of concentrated Ethyl Fluid shipments to both Japan and the Soviet Union.

subfiles.title: Moseley memorandum of Kellogg press inquiry
subfiles.about: Records a journalist’s inquiry about aviation-gasoline policy and rumors of a gasoline embargo.
subfiles.summary: G. T. Kellogg of National Petroleum News asked about the government policy on delivering technical information needed for high-quality aviation gasoline. Moseley referred him to a New York Herald Tribune article and said he knew of no contemplated embargo procedure beyond press references to a possible Pittman bill and Henry L. Stimson’s letter to the New York Times.

subfiles.title: Senator Byrd letter forwarding Chilton’s protest
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent’s objection to petroleum shipments to Japan and Russia.
subfiles.summary: Byrd sends Hull a letter from Samuel B. Chilton, editor of the Southern Churchman. He asks that the complaint about petroleum trade with Japan and Russia receive the Secretary’s consideration.

subfiles.title: Chilton letter opposing petroleum trade with Japan and Russia
subfiles.about: Urges an end to American petroleum trade supporting Japan’s war in China and the Soviet attack on Finland.
subfiles.summary: Chilton cites H. V. Kaltenborn’s broadcast alleging daily West Coast petroleum sales for Japanese and Soviet military use. Arguing that the United States should support democracy, he asks Byrd to work for an end to the trade in war materials with both countries.

subfiles.title: Hull reply to Senator Byrd concerning Chilton’s letter
subfiles.about: Provides the Department’s standard legal response to requests for an end to petroleum exports and returns Chilton’s letter.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges Chilton’s opposition to petroleum trade with Japan and the Soviet Union and thanks Byrd for forwarding the letter. The reply states that no statute then authorized the proposed prohibition and notes that no petroleum products had been exported from the United States to the Soviet Union during December 1939 or January 1940 to date. Chilton’s letter is returned.

subfiles.title: Senator Byrd letter forwarding Kennedy’s appeal
subfiles.about: Forwards a clergyman’s appeal for an embargo on war materials sold to Japan and requests comment.
subfiles.summary: Byrd says he is receiving many letters like the enclosed communication from the Reverend J. W. Kennedy. He asks Hull to comment on the issue raised by the correspondence.

subfiles.title: Kennedy letter urging an embargo on Japan
subfiles.about: Calls for the immediate termination of American material support for Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: Kennedy cites missionaries’ accounts of conditions in China and claims that the United States supplies 61 percent of Japan’s war materials. Writing as a voter, taxpayer, and Christian, he urges Byrd to use every effective means to end those sales.

subfiles.title: Hull reply to Senator Byrd concerning Kennedy’s letter
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Kennedy’s embargo appeal and supplies the Department’s usual response.
subfiles.summary: Hull thanks Byrd for forwarding Kennedy’s request for an embargo on war-material exports to Japan. The letter indicates that the Department’s standard legal explanation is being provided and returns Kennedy’s correspondence.

subfiles.title: E. B. Badger letter suspending negotiations under the moral embargo
subfiles.from: E. B. Badger and Sons Company
subfiles.about: Reports suspension of negotiations involving aviation-gasoline technology while raising concern about the company’s legal position.
subfiles.summary: Badger acknowledges the Department’s request that companies withhold plans, plants, manufacturing rights, and technical information needed for high-quality aviation gasoline from certain countries. It says that relevant negotiations have been suspended for the time being. The company nevertheless expresses serious uncertainty about its legal position and assumes that the Department and Congress will take appropriate action.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck memorandum of conversation with Buffum
subfiles.about: Records advice to an American businessman considering a return to Japan amid tightening economic pressure.
subfiles.summary: Buffum sought personal and business advice on returning to Japan, where he had a partnership connected with gasoline fuels. Hornbeck saw no immediate personal-safety reason not to return but warned that future business conditions depended on Japanese conduct. He explained that continued mistreatment of American nationals and interests could lead the United States to apply one or more forms of pressure against Japan.

subfiles.title: Green memorandum arranging Buffum’s meeting with Hornbeck
subfiles.about: Records George Hargrove’s request that Hornbeck meet Buffum before Buffum returned to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hargrove explained that the Tapsumi Engineering Company acted as E. B. Badger’s Japanese agent and that its American partner, Buffum, was then in the United States. Green consulted Hornbeck and arranged for Buffum to make an appointment during the following week.

subfiles.title: Phillips Petroleum agreement to submit monthly reports
subfiles.from: K. S. Adams, Phillips Petroleum Company
subfiles.about: Agrees to furnish monthly information on blending-agent sales and deliveries for export to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Adams accepts Green’s request for regular export reporting. Phillips Petroleum promises to submit each month’s Japanese blending-agent sales and deliveries by the fifteenth day of the following month.
